The 1896 Summer Olympics. The first modern Olympic Games, held in Athens, Greece, revived the ancient Greek athletic competition as an international event. In April 1896, about two hundred and forty athletes from fourteen nations participated—a modest start by modern standards. The host nation Greece benefited greatly from home advantage, finishing at the top of the medal count with ten gold medals.

These Games revived an ancient tradition. The original Olympic competition had last been held in 393 of the Common Era, nearly fifteen hundred years earlier. Baron Pierre de Coubertin, who founded the International Olympic Committee, believed athletic competition could foster peace and international understanding.

The 1896 Games established many features that would shape the modern Olympics. The program was diverse, including track and field, gymnastics, weightlifting, wrestling, and shooting. The marathon was run for the first time, commemorating the legendary run of a Greek soldier from Marathon to Athens bearing news of victory. American athletes dominated in many events, particularly in track and field, establishing the United States as an Olympic power from the very outset.

One notable absence shaped these Games as much as what was present. Women were prohibited from competing—the Games were entirely male-only, a reflection of Victorian attitudes toward sport and gender that would only gradually change in the decades to come.
